es.summary: El estreñimiento se define como menos de tres evacuaciones semanales con heces duras y dolorosas. Es frecuente y suele responder a cambios en la dieta, hidratación y actividad física.
key_points: Factores modificables: fibra, líquidos, ejercicio y uso de laxantes.
Medicamentos como opioides y anticolinérgicos pueden precipitarlo.
Complicaciones incluyen impactación fecal, hemorroides y desequilibrio electrolítico.

pathophysiology: Reducción del contenido de agua y fibra ralentiza el tránsito colónico.
Absorción excesiva de agua produce heces secas y compactas.
El aumento del tono del esfínter anal y el esfuerzo aumentan el dolor.
risk_factors: Uso de opioides, anticolinérgicos o suplementos de hierro.
signs_symptoms: Heces duras, secas y en forma de bolitas.
diagnostics: Historia clínica y registro de patrón de evacuación.
Radiografía de abdomen si se sospecha impactación fecal.
Electrolitos séricos si hay uso prolongado de laxantes (K+, Na+).
treatment: Aumento de fibra dietética (frutas, verduras, granos integrales).
Laxantes formadores de masa: psyllium, metilcelulosa.
Laxantes osmóticos (lactulosa) o estimulantes (senna) si persiste.
complications: Hemorroides y fisura anal por esfuerzo excesivo.
nursing_care: Evaluar frecuencia, consistencia (Escala de Bristol) y esfuerzo.
Monitorear ingesta de líquidos y fibra.
Promover ambulación y ejercicios de abdomen.
Administrar laxantes según prescripción y observar respuesta.
patient_teaching: Incluir al menos 25 g de fibra dietética diaria.
Beber ≥2 L de agua al día, especialmente al usar laxantes.
Establecer horarios regulares para ir al baño sin apresurarse.
Evitar la retención de la necesidad de evacuar.
Usar laxantes solo bajo indicación médica y no prolongadamente.

outcomes: Patrón de evacuación intestinal: ≥3 evacuaciones semanales sin esfuerzo excesivo
Consistencia de heces: tipo 3‑4 en escala de Bristol
Dolor abdominal durante la evacuación: ausente o ≤2/10

interventions.action: Evaluar y registrar patrón de evacuación y consistencia de heces cada 24 h
interventions.rationale: Permite identificar mejoría o deterioro y ajustar el plan de cuidados

interventions.action: Educar al paciente sobre aumento de fibra dietética y consumo de agua
interventions.rationale: La fibra y la hidratación suavizan las heces y facilitan el tránsito

interventions.action: Promover la movilización temprana y ejercicios abdominales
interventions.rationale: La actividad física estimula la motilidad intestinal

interventions.action: Administrar docusato según prescripción y observar efecto en 24‑48 h
interventions.rationale: Suaviza las heces sin causar dependencia

interventions.action: Reforzar la necesidad de acudir al baño cuando surge la urgencia, sin retrasar
interventions.rationale: Evita la retención que empeora el estreñimiento

related_to: deshidratación por ingesta insuficiente de líquidos
outcomes: Electrolitos séricos (Na+, K+) dentro de rangos normales
Estado de hidratación: ingesta y salida de líquidos equilibradas

interventions.action: Monitorear signos vitales y balance hídrico cada turno
interventions.rationale: Detecta precozmente deshidratación o alteraciones electrolíticas

interventions.action: Obtener y registrar niveles de electrolitos cada 48 h mientras se usan laxantes
interventions.rationale: Permite identificar desequilibrios y ajustar tratamiento

interventions.action: Educar al paciente sobre la importancia de ingerir al menos 2 L de agua al día
interventions.rationale: Previene la pérdida de electrolitos y la deshidratación

interventions.action: Revisar la medicación del paciente para identificar fármacos constipantes
interventions.rationale: Reducir la exposición a agentes que puedan requerir laxantes

interventions.action: Enseñar el uso correcto de laxantes, evitando dosis excesivas o uso prolongado
interventions.rationale: Minimiza el riesgo de pérdida de electrolitos y dependencia

en.summary: Constipation is defined as fewer than three bowel movements per week with hard, painful stools. It is common and usually responds to dietary changes, hydration, and physical activity.
key_points: Frequency <3 bowel movements/week is the diagnostic criterion.
Modifiable factors: fiber, fluids, exercise, and laxant use.
Medications such as opioids and anticholinergics can precipitate it.
Complications include fecal impaction, hemorrhoids, and electrolyte imbalance.

pathophysiology: Reduced water and fiber content slows colonic transit.
Excessive water absorption produces dry, compact stools.
Increased anal sphincter tone and straining increase pain.
risk_factors: Use of opioids, anticholinergics, or iron supplements.
signs_symptoms: Fewer than 3 bowel movements per week.
diagnostics: Medical history and bowel pattern charting.
Abdominal X‑ray if fecal impaction is suspected.
Serum electrolytes if prolonged laxant use (K+, Na+).
treatment: Increase dietary fiber (fruits, vegetables, whole grains).
Drink ≥2 L of water per day.
Osmotic (lactulose) or stimulant (senna) laxatives if needed.
complications: Hemorrhoids and anal fissure from excessive straining.
nursing_care: Assess frequency, consistency (Bristol Scale), and straining.
Administer laxatives as prescribed and observe response.
patient_teaching: Include at least 25 g of dietary fiber daily.
Drink ≥2 L of water daily, especially when using laxatives.
Establish regular bathroom times without rushing.
Avoid withholding the urge to evacuate.
Use laxatives only under medical guidance and not for prolonged periods.

outcomes: Bowel pattern: ≥3 bowel movements per week without excessive straining
Stool consistency: type 3‑4 on Bristol Scale
Abdominal pain during evacuation: absent or ≤2/10

interventions.action: Assess and record bowel pattern and stool consistency every 24 h
interventions.rationale: Allows identification of improvement or deterioration and adjustment of care plan

interventions.action: Educate patient on increasing dietary fiber and fluid intake
interventions.rationale: Fiber and hydration soften stools and facilitate transit

interventions.action: Promote early mobilization and abdominal exercises
interventions.rationale: Physical activity stimulates intestinal motility

interventions.action: Administer docusate as prescribed and observe effect in 24‑48 h
interventions.rationale: Softens stools without causing dependence

interventions.action: Reinforce the need to use the bathroom promptly when the urge arises, without delay
interventions.rationale: Prevents withholding that worsens constipation

outcomes: Serum electrolytes (Na+, K+) within normal ranges
Hydration status: fluid intake and output balanced

interventions.action: Monitor vital signs and fluid balance each shift
interventions.rationale: Early detection of dehydration or electrolyte disturbances

interventions.action: Obtain and record electrolyte levels every 48 h while using laxatives
interventions.rationale: Identifies imbalances and allows treatment adjustment

interventions.action: Educate patient on the importance of ingesting at least 2 L of water daily
interventions.rationale: Prevents electrolyte loss and dehydration

interventions.action: Review patient medication list to identify constipating drugs
interventions.rationale: Reduce exposure to agents that may require laxatives

interventions.action: Teach proper laxative use, avoiding excessive doses or prolonged use
interventions.rationale: Minimizes risk of electrolyte loss and dependence

Pharmacology for Nurses: Laxatives and Stool Softeners

summary.0.quote: Constipation means having fewer than three bowel movements a week. The stool (poop) can be hard and dry.

key_points.1.quote: They include: Eating more fruits, vegetables and grains, which are high in fiber Drinking plenty of water and other liquids Getting enough exercise Taking time to have a bowel movement when you need to Using laxatives only if your health care provider says you should

key_points.2.quote: Certain medications can also promote constipation, such as anticholinergics and opioids.

sections.pathophysiology.0.quote: It can be caused by slowed peristalsis caused by decreased activity, dehydration, lack of fiber, medications (e.g., opioids, diuretics), depression, or abdominal surgical procedures.

sections.pathophysiology.1.quote: As the stool moves slowly through the large intestine , additional water is reabsorbed, resulting in the stool becoming hard, dry, and difficult to move through the lower intestines.

sections.risk_factors.2.quote: It often results from low fiber intake, dehydration, and a sedentary lifestyle.

sections.signs_symptoms.2.quote: The straining with defecation can lead to complications such as a hemorrhoids (swollen and inflamed vein in the rectum and anus that can cause discomfort, itching, and bleeding) or an anal fissure (a small tear or cut in the lining of the anus, which can cause pain, bleeding, and discomfort during bowel movements).

sections.signs_symptoms.3.quote: Constipation is an unpleasant symptom or disorder that results in difficult stool evacuation or irregular and inconsistent stool passage, with common complaints like straining, incomplete or difficulty passing stools, or not defecating for a prolonged time.

sections.signs_symptoms.4.quote: The accumulation of stool in the colon can also lead to distension, gas, and bloating (sensation of fullness or swelling in the abdomen), contributing to abdominal discomfort.

sections.diagnostics.0.quote: Figure 27.6 The Bristol Stool Chart is used to assess the characteristics of stools according to seven types, ranging from constipation to diarrhea.

sections.treatment.0.quote: Nurses provide personalized guidance on dietary modifications, emphasizing the importance of incorporating fruits, vegetables, whole grains, and other high-fiber foods into daily meals.

sections.treatment.4.quote: Bulk-forming laxatives containing fiber (e.g., psyllium powder [Metamucil], methylcellulose [Citrucel]) increase the bulk and water content of stool, facilitating its passage.

sections.complications.0.quote: Chronic constipation may result in fecal impaction , where a large mass of hardened stool becomes lodged in the rectum, resulting in a palpable abdominal mass and rectal pressure due to the buildup of stool, making it difficult or impossible to pass stool normally (Clevelan

sections.complications.1.quote: The straining with defecation can lead to complications such as a hemorrhoids (swollen and inflamed vein in the rectum and anus that can cause discomfort, itching, and bleeding) or an anal fissure (a small tear or cut in the lining of the anus, which can cause pain, bleeding, and discomfort during bowel movements).

sections.complications.3.quote: Fecal incontinence can be caused by a variety of factors, including the following: ongoing (chronic) constipation, causing the anus muscles and intestines to stretch and weaken, leading to diarrhea and stool leakage fecal impaction with a lump of hard stool that partly blocks the large intestine long-term laxative use colectomy or bowel surgery lack of sensation of the need to have a bowel movement gynecological, prostate, or rectal surgery injur

sections.nursing_care.0.quote: Assess client’s bowel habits including frequency, consistency, and ease of bowel movements.

sections.nursing_care.1.quote: The client taking a laxative or a stool softener should: Increase their dietary intake of fiber and increase their fluid intake, if not contraindicated, to help reduce the risk of constipation.

sections.patient_teaching.4.quote: While laxatives can provide relief from constipation, they should be used cautiously and under the guidance of a healthcare provider to avoid dependence and potential complications, and they are typically recommended for short-term use rather than as long-term solutions.
